catalog_quote: Coptic words are always stressed on one of the last two syllables. Since Coptic word stress is intermingled with vowel quality and quantity to a high degree, it depends a lot on the interpretation of the vowel system whether stress in Coptic is to be considered bound or free. ... Word stress is not indicated in the indigenous Egyptian scripts. Our opinions about stress in Egyptian are therefore based largely on speculation. It is generally assumed that the stress position in a word as evidenced from Coptic was the same in the earlier language (at least as far back as the Paleo-Coptic stage). In the conventional Paleo-Coptic reconstruction stress is therefore assumed to have fallen on one of the last two syllables in a word. In the revised Paleo-Coptic reconstruction as proposed in this book, it must be assumed that stress either falls on the penult or on the antepenult syllable of a wor…
sweep_summary: Both works with stress in the title (Aylett & Turk 2004, Language and Speech; Turk 2010, Laboratory Phonology) are Glottolog misattributions to egyp1246: their abstracts (downloaded from PubMed efetch and Crossref, show they are about English spontaneous speech and general prosodic-constituency theory, with nothing on Egyptian or Coptic; priority none. Heidelberg digi now behind an Anubis bot wall; SAGE 403; De Gruyter 202). The best first-hand statement read is the catalog's own deciding source, Peust 1999 §6.1.6-§6.1.7 pp. 273-274 (held scan, page render p274 checked by eye): stress unwritten in Egyptian scripts, inferred from Coptic; window = last two syllables (conventional) or penult/antepenult (Peust's revised reconstruction); position within the window not predictable, so stress phonemic in Egyptian on the majority view (Knudsen 1962 dissenting). This confirms and slightly refines the catalog's 'lexical' coding; it does not supersede the deciding source.

new_statements.quote: In the conventional Paleo-Coptic reconstruction stress is therefore assumed to have fallen on one of the last two syllables in a word. In the revised Paleo-Coptic reconstruction as proposed in this book, it must be assumed that stress either falls on the penult or on the antepenult syllable of a word. [...] On the other hand, most modern scholars assume that the Paleo-Coptic vowel inventory was similar or identical in stressed and unstressed syllables (§ 5.8.1). If this is true, we can conclude that stress was phonemic in Egyptian.

new_statements.locator: §6.1.7 'Stress in Pre-Coptic Egyptian', p. 274 (cf. §6.1.6 p. 273, §6.1.5 p. 273)
new_statements.reading: For pre-Coptic Egyptian (the egyp1246 entity proper) Peust says stress is not written and is inferred from Coptic; the position is confined to a two-syllable window (last two syllables in the conventional reconstruction; penult or antepenult in Peust's own revised reconstruction), and within that window it is not predictable from segmental structure, so stress was phonemic/distinctive in Egyptian on the majority view (§6.1.6 adds Coptic near-minimal pairs and notes Knudsen 1962 as the dissenting non-phonemic analysis). This is the same source as the catalog's deciding quotation and supports the 'lexical' coding; the fuller §6.1.7 passage refines it by stating the window explicitly (penult/antepenult in the revised reconstruction) and by making the phonemic-stress conclusion explicit.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: both deciding passages and the exceptions sentence are verbatim on the page images we hold of Peust 1999 pp. 273-274 at the stated section numbers; the full 365-page scan and scanned are also held locally (our earlier reading cache). Deciding source: a dedicated phonology monograph (1999) that is the standard reference for Egyptian-Coptic phonology; the Glottolog descriptive list contains only grammars and sketches, none with better stress coverage.
